articles.title: The Trump administration wants to take greater control of scientific grants. Here’s why that’s a terrible idea
articles.description: Since World War II, the United States has dominated science and technology. With more than 400 Nobel Prizes, it dwarfs every other country. Major breakthroughs like nuclear energy, genetic engineering, and the internet were all led by researchers and engineers in the U.S. Today, it leads in every major technological category. To a great extent, this has been the result of government action. Federal agencies such as the NIH, NSF, and DARPA spearheaded many of the most advanced technologies, and U.S. research universities have become beacons for top scientific talent. These advances have brought us greater prosperity, better health, and enhanced well-being. That’s why the recent news of an executive order that would give political oversight to scientific grants provoked such an uproar. Although the administration quickly backed off, the incident represents a troubling trend of political interference in science that has led to a major brain drain of scientific talent. Without a major change in course, the damage could be permanent. Science, The Endless Frontier America wasn’t always a scientific mecca. In fact, at the beginning of the 20th century, bright young students often had to go to Europe to pursue advanced degrees in the sciences because American universities were considered second-rate. Yet as the U.S. industrialized, that began to change and, by the 1930s, with Europe increasingly in turmoil, world-class scientific talent began to flock to American shores. In 1940, Vannevar Bush, who at the time was serving as president of the Carnegie Institution for Science, went to see President Roosevelt. His proposal led to the establishment of the Office of Scientific Research and Development (OSRD), which mobilized the country’s scientific resources for World War II. It was, by all accounts, a resounding success, resulting in breakthroughs such as radar, penicillin, the proximity fuse and, most famously, the atomic bomb. As the war was winding down, Roosevelt asked Bush to write a report proposing how America could continue the success of the OSRD in peacetime. That report, Science: The Endless Frontier, was delivered to President Truman in 1945 and would set the stage for America’s technological dominance during the second half of the century. Bush wrote: “Basic research leads to new knowledge. It provides scientific capital. It creates the fund from which the practical applications of knowledge must be drawn. New products and new processes do not appear full-grown. They are founded on new principles and new conceptions, which in turn are painstakingly developed by research in the purest realms of science.” It was that vision that led to U.S. technological dominance. Look at any major technology we use today—whether it is the internet, GPS, or lithium-ion batteries—and the initial breakthrough came from government funding. A study from the Institute for New Economic Thinking found that every new drug approved between 2010 and 2019 benefited from government grants. Even major private firms, such as Google and Qualcomm, started out with government funding. A key tenet of that vision is that decisions about research grants be made by scientists, not political appointees, so that we are funding scientific, not political priorities. That principle is what has come under threat. The Visceral Abstract There is a long history of politicians being hostile to science. In a 2012 interview, then-Sen. and current Secretary of State Marco Rubio said that the age of the universe and the Big Bang “has zero to do with how our economy is going to grow.” Former Vice President Mike Pence expressed doubts about Darwin’s theory of natural selection. Paul Broun, a former Georgia congressman, called it “lies straight from the pit of hell.” Yet the Big Bang is not just a theory, but the result of a set of theories, including general relativity and quantum mechanics, combined with many observations over a period of decades. Darwin’s theory is core to our understanding of life sciences. Students learn about these things not to shape their religious beliefs, but because they underlie basic scientific work. Politicians attack science because it’s an easy target. It’s not hard for the public to imagine that their tax dollars are funding overeducated elites thinking up wacky theories in ivory-tower institutions. Scientific theories take time and effort to understand and can be maddeningly difficult to explain. The truth is that we live in a world of the visceral abstract, where strange theories underlie much of our everyday existence. Technologies that we use every day, such as the lasers that scan our purchases in the checkout aisle and the semiconductors that drive our devices, arose from these same strange ideas. Darwin’s theory underlies everything from fighting diseases like COVID-19 to guiding logistics systems. If we are to master the advanced technologies of the future—such as quantum computing, synthetic biology, and materials science—we need to master the scientific theories that will drive them. The Tragedy of Trofim Lysenko While Vannevar Bush showed what can be achieved when a government invests in science as a public good, Trofim Lysenko showed what happens when science is politicized. A Soviet agronomist who considered the concept of a gene a “bourgeois invention,” Lysenko—like Pence and Broun—was skeptical of Darwin’s theories. Yet he was able to get Joseph Stalin to support his ideas—such as his theory that exposing seeds to low temperatures will help them grow in the winter—which were mainly based on political expediency and personal belief, not on empirical evidence. He promised miracle crop yields that never materialized, but his power allowed him to suppress legitimate scientists. The effect on Soviet biological science was chilling. Anybody reporting results that contradicted Lysenko’s theories risked not only professional suicide but, in many cases, imprisonment and even execution. To adopt “bourgeois” science was not just to have a different idea, but to be branded an “enemy of the people” working to undermine the Soviet project. Meanwhile, those who went along with Lysenko’s program gained authority, and competency in Soviet biological sciences was greatly undermined. Crop yields steadily declined throughout the late 1930s until his downfall in the mid-1960s. Many believe that his theories contributed to the Great Famine in China. If Nothing Is True, Everything Is Possible One thing that struck me during the 15 years I lived in post-communist countries was how problems seemed to build on themselves. In Kraków, the abandoned frame of the Szkieletor building stood frozen for decades. Construction had stalled in the 1970s, so the frame just stood there rusting. It became almost a metaphor for the Soviet space as a whole. In a healthy society with checks and balances, someone would have been brought to account. There would have been litigation. A court would have mandated a cleanup. But in a command economy, power flows from a single source, with no one to hold it accountable. Those in power don’t have to admit their mistakes. Questions of truth become questions of loyalty. We have a similar process underway in the U.S. When politicians and unelected bureaucrats seek to make scientific funding conform to their ideological preferences, they are not merely making budget allocations. They are seeking to control what is true and what is not. We’ve seen this enough times before to know how it ends. America achieved technological dominance, in part, because of the scientists who fled Europe to escape similar populist tyranny. Now, that process is reversing, with scientists leaving America for Europe. The advantages we built after World War II are quickly eroding, threatening our prosperity and security. That’s why we don’t want politicians running science. It diminishes science and leaves us with only politics.

articles.title: The list of AI insiders sounding the alarm on their own companies keeps growing
articles.description: Last week, OpenAI safety leader David Robinson resigned from the company, becoming the latest to join what is, in his words, a “parade of former colleagues” who have left roles at AI companies amid concerns about the tech or its use. In a subsequent essay for The Atlantic, he said the “trial and error” approach favored by AI companies must end. Robinson is far from alone. Here’s a list of other AI researchers and employees who’ve made public warnings about their former employers. ED NEWTON-REX In November 2023, Ed Newton-Rex left his role leading the audio team at Stability AI, the maker of text-to-image tool Stable Diffusion, over concerns about the way copyrighted material was being used to train the tech. “My opinion here doesn’t align with the generative AI industry’s current way of doing things,” Newton-Rex told Fast Company following his resignation, adding that he thought the industry’s prevailing outlook, paired with rapidly advancing tech, would be “very, very bad for creators.” Since then, he’s founded Fairly Trained, a nonprofit that issues certifications for AI companies whose data use meets certain requirements. THE GROUP LETTER On June 4, 2024, 13 current and former employees of top AI companies published a letter titled “A Right to Warn about Advanced Artificial Intelligence.” In it, they asserted that the technology poses risks ranging from “the further entrenchment of existing inequalities, to manipulation and misinformation, to the loss of control of autonomous AI systems potentially resulting in human extinction,” and expressed concerns about a lack of oversight. Signatories included former Google DeepMind employee Ramana Kumar, former Anthropic and current Google DeepMind employee Neel Nanda, who leads the company’s mechanistic interpretability team; and 11 current and former OpenAI employees, including Jacob Hilton, who now works for the Alignment Research Center; Daniel Kokotajlo, who founded and leads the nonprofit research group AI Futures Project; William Saunders, Carroll Wainwright, and Daniel Ziegler, the latter of whom now works for Anthropic; and six people who remained anonymous. Prominent computer scientists Yoshua Bengio, Stuart Russell, and “Godfather of AI” Geoffrey Hinton also endorsed the letter. JAN LEIKE In May 2024, OpenAI Superalignment team lead Jan Leike announced his departure on X, stating that “safety culture and processes have taken a backseat to shiny products.” Leike, who has also worked at Google’s DeepMind, now heads Anthropic’s alignment team. “Now is a good time to build institutional mechanisms to pace the frontier of AI development,” he said on X in September. “The industry is locked into an all-out scaling race to build superintelligence as quickly as possible, and we may need to give everyone more time for safety and alignment mitigations.” Leike added, “I’m not the only one who believes this,” linking to a statement titled “Pacing the Frontier” signed by 1,386 employees of major AI companies. SUCHIR BALAJI After graduating from the University of California, Berkeley, Suchir Balaji was hired by OpenAI, where he spent about four years working on ChatGPT and other projects. He left the company in August 2024, on the same day as cofounder John Schulman, who said the timing was coincidental. Balaji blew the whistle on what he said were copyright infringements by Open AI, and published an essay online explaining how he thought ChatGPT’s outputs violated Fair Use law. That November, he was named as a potential witness in The New York Times’s lawsuit against OpenAI alleging willful copyright infringement. The 26-year-old was found dead in his San Francisco apartment eight days later. His death was ruled a suicide, though his parents and others raised questions about that determination, as reported by The Guardian. MRINANK SHARMA In February, Mrinank Sharma announced his departure from Anthropic, where he led the Safeguards Research team. “I continuously find myself reckoning with our situation,” Sharma wrote in his resignation letter, which he shared on X. “The world is in peril,” he continued, not just from AI and bioweapons, but “a whole series of interconnected crises.” ALEX TURNER Alex Turner left his job as a Google DeepMind research scientist in June, after a failed campaign to stop the company from signing a contract that allows the U.S. Pentagon to use its AI “for any lawful government purpose,” which he and others worry may allow for mass surveillance and autonomous weapons. Last month, he testified for a U.S. Senate hearing on rogue AI. “Often we think about the movements of our overseas adversaries, but now we must consider how we may be building adversaries at home by training misaligned AI systems,” he said in his written statement. JACOB COXON Jacob Coxon, a former researcher for OpenAI and Anthropic, resigned from the latter last month. “Neither company is acting responsibly,” he said in a viral X post. “They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.” He went on to assert that “the people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade.” In an interview with PBS in September, Coxon said an AI race with China “could be very bad, and that we should be taking pretty rapid actions for international coordination,” but that he believes the company leaders echoing that desire “are privately quite skeptical” of being able to achieve that cooperation. MIKITA BALESNI, TOMEK KORBAK, AND JASMINE WANG Last week, three OpenAI safety and alignment researchers were fired for mishandling sensitive misinformation, which one of them, Tomek Korbak, said online was due to how he’d communicated information to METR, the AI research nonprofit investigating OpenAI’s recent Hugging Face hacking incident. “AI is not a normal technology, and OpenAI is not a normal company,” the researchers said in the letter they sent to company leadership, which they published online on October 8. “Those of us who work on safety see risks before anyone else, and we rely on close collaboration with outside experts to work out how to address them. The freedom to do so without fear, and to have well-defined internal procedures that enable this work, is itself an essential safety mechanism.” OpenAI released a statement the following day saying the researchers were fired after an internal investigation “found they violated clear policies on handling sensitive information,” adding, “We want to be very clear that these decisions were not about raising safety concerns or speaking out.”

articles.title: Ubuntu Confirms Thursday's Distributed Denial of Service Attack Against Its Web Infrastructure
articles.description: On Thursday those trying to access the Ubuntu website, ISO downloads, and similar Ubuntu resources on Thursday found the site "inoperable," reports Phoronix, with the disruption confirmed as a distributed denial of service attack. "Our team is working diligently to resolve the incident," according to a Thursday post on Ubuntu Discourse — followed by a later announcement. "At this time our team continues to work on restoring affected services, most of them are now available. We appreciate your patience and understanding." Ubuntu's status page shows the Ubuntu.com outage lasting for 2 hours and 27 minutes on Friday — though with four-hour outages Wednesday (and other outages affecting other Ubuntu sites). Today "All components are Operational," the status page reports. Read more of this story at Slashdot.
